new_statements.quote: Languages in Zone C share a generally uncomplicated typology according to Guthrie (1948): ",..the principal features of the languages of this zone are a simpler grammatical structure than is found in many others, coupled with a simple phonological and tonal system. [...]" [...] The languages of Zone C are listed below: (10) Ngundi Group (11) Ngondi (Ngundi). (12) Pande (Ndjeli, Linyeli, Linzeli)-Bogongo (Bukongo, Bongili), 1,000 speakers of Pande alone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Zone C Bantu languages (Ngondi among them) are said, after Guthrie 1948, to have a simple tonal system, i.e. they are tone languages; no stress information.
new_statements.identity_note: Guthrie's C.11 Ngondi of the Ngundi Group (10), 'spoken in Congo (Brazzaville) and the Central African Republic' = Ngundi [ndn]; not the Ubangian Gundi [gdi]. Group-level statement (Bantu Zone C, quoting Guthrie 1948), secondhand. [name in source: Ngondi (Ngundi); pages 104-105 (Zone C)]

sources.citation: Leblanc, Simon (compilateur; avec Annette Harrison, Pauline Linton, Angi Ngumbu, Ruth Raharimanantsoa et al.). 2012. Le développement des langues de la République du Congo : État des travaux. Version 1.6, octobre 2012. Brazzaville: SIL Groupe Afrique centrale - Congo. 138 pp. (Glottolog ref 476737.) Entry 'Ngundi' [ndn] C11, p. 67.
sources.note: Nothing on stress, accent or tone: the Ngundi entry is empty in every rubric except Lexicographie (Ouzilleau 1911 short vocabulary); the only phonetic content is the pronunciation of the glossonym [ŋgu.ndi]. Confirms first-hand (SIL-Congo, 2012) that no survey, grammar or phonology of Ngundi [ndn] existed.

sources.citation: Grégoire, Claire. 2003. The Bantu languages of the forest. In Nurse & Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 349-370. London: Routledge. §2.3 Tonality (p. 357).
sources.note: Family-level only: 'the C10 and C20 languages do not display these particularities, as far as their tone systems are known. Aka (C10), Koyo (C24) and Mboshi (C25), for instance, have a tone system of the classical type.' Ngundi C11 is not named; nothing about stress/accent.

sources.citation: Royal Museum for Central Africa (Tervuren). n.d. [online 'lexico' data sheet] Bantu C11 Ngondi: data collected for Bastin Y., Coupez A. & Mann M. 1999, Continuity and divergence in the Bantu languages: perspectives from a lexicostatistic study. 7 pp., 80 numbered items (01 'all'.. 92 'woman'), source column 'lexico : Voeltz 1990' on every row (= Erhard F. K. Voeltz, unpublished 1990 lexical questionnaire for Ngondi of Nola-Berberati, C11).
sources.note: No prose at all. The 80 forms are tone-marked (grave/acute diacritics, partly garbled by the sheet's legacy font, e.g. 14 cloud 'kùt_u, Bà-', 09 black 'kp_Okp_o', 88 water 'mà`Kk_o, Bà-'), which shows Voeltz transcribed lexical tone for Ngondi in 1990, but nothing is stated about tone rules, accent or stress. Value: it identifies the only modern first-hand phonetic transcription of [ndn] besides the 40-item ASJP list -- Voeltz's 1990 questionnaire held at Tervuren -- as a print/archive pointer.

sources.citation: Johnston, Harry H. 1919. A comparative study of the Bantu and Semi-Bantu languages, vol. 1. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Group SS 'Kadei-Lobai (Upper Sanga) languages', no. 222 'Gundi or Ba-gundu' (vocabulary column and prefix table; source note p. 813: column taken from Ouzilleau 1911).
sources.note: Nothing on accent, stress or tone; comparative vocabulary tables and a prefix list only. Listed so it is not re-chased: it adds no data beyond Ouzilleau 1911.

sources.citation: Ouzilleau, [Dr F.]. 1911. Notes sur la langue des Pygmées de la Sanga, suivies de dix vocabulaires. Revue d'ethnographie et de sociologie 2: 75-92.
sources.note: Nothing. Comparative wordlists; Vocabulaire III pairs a 'Négrille' (Baka) list with a 'Gundi' (= Ngundi C11) column from Bakoto, a Gundi village on the Sanga below Nola. The only prosodic remark in the article is Johnston's second-hand comment on pygmy 'staccato' pronunciation in general, not about Gundi.
